passage:
For a whole week, Lavanya had copied the long-division answers from Ramu's slate in the little school behind the panchayat office. She didn't understand where the numbers went. Asking felt impossible; last year a boy had called her "duffer" when she asked a question, and the whole row had laughed.

On Friday, when the others ran out to the handpump, she stayed back. Not the loud Sir who taught science. Nandini Madam, who never laughed at anyone. Lavanya twisted her dupatta. "Madam… I need help. I don't get the dividing."

Nandini Madam put down her chalk. "Thank you for telling me. That takes courage. Come, sit. And I think half the class needs this too." On Monday she taught it again, slowly, for everyone.

qa.q: Whose slate had Lavanya been copying from?
qa.a: Ramu's slate.

qa.q: Why had Lavanya avoided asking for a week?
qa.a: She was afraid of being judged and laughed at, because last year a boy called her "duffer" when she asked and the whole row laughed.

qa.q: What did Lavanya do that was wise when she finally asked?
qa.a: She chose a safe person, Nandini Madam, who never laughed at anyone, and asked in private when the others had gone out.

qa.q: How did Nandini Madam see Lavanya's request?
qa.a: As courage, not weakness; she thanked her and guessed others needed help too, so she retaught it for everyone.

grounding: It shows a child who feared being judged finally saying she needs help to a trusted teacher, and the teacher treating it as a strength.

passage:
"Mummy, may I go to Tanya's party on Saturday? It's at the play zone in the big mall. Everyone's going by auto together."

Parul looked up from her laptop. "What time does it end?"
"Eight… or nine."
"And who's bringing you back?"
Sangeeta shrugged. "We'll share an auto."

Parul shook her head. "Then my answer is no to the auto, and here's why: it'll be dark, I don't know the other parents yet, and four eleven-year-olds alone in an auto at nine isn't safe. But yes to the party if I drop you and pick you up at eight-thirty."

Sangeeta groaned. "So embarrassing." Then she thought. "Can you wait outside the gate, not inside?"
"Deal."

qa.q: Where was Tanya's party?
qa.a: At the play zone in the big mall.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when she groaned, "So embarrassing"?
qa.a: Disappointed and a little embarrassed at being dropped and picked up by her mother, though she accepted because she still got to go.

qa.q: Why did Parul's answer make the no easier to accept?
qa.a: She gave clear reasons, the dark, not knowing the parents and safety, and offered a yes to the party with a safer plan.

qa.q: How might Parul feel about making the pickup deal?
qa.a: She probably feels relieved that Sangeeta can go safely and is willing to wait outside the gate to spare her embarrassment.

grounding: It shows a child asking permission and a parent explaining a partial no with clear safety reasons, which helps the child accept it.

passage:
Group-work note, Monday, from Tushar (science teacher, Class 5)

Sunaina's group was building the solar-system model today, and within five minutes she was giving orders: "You paint Saturn. No, not like that. Sit there. Give me the glue." Two members went silent, and Aman pushed his chair back.

I noticed Sunaina kept glancing at the clock and whispering, "We'll never finish." It looked less like bossiness and more like worry. I took her aside and suggested swapping orders for invitations: "How about we…?" She tried it straight away: "How about we do the rings together, Aman?" Aman pulled his chair back in. I'll check on the group again on Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Sunaina's group building?
qa.a: The solar-system model.

qa.q: What was Sunaina likely feeling behind her orders?
qa.a: Anxious that the group wouldn't finish in time; her glances at the clock suggest the orders came from worry more than a wish to boss people.

qa.q: What did Tushar coach Sunaina to try?
qa.a: Swapping orders for invitations such as "How about we…?", which she used straight away with Aman.

qa.q: How did the group members feel about the orders?
qa.a: They felt pushed aside and upset: two went silent and Aman pushed his chair back.

grounding: It is a teacher's note on a child's bossy commands coming from worry, and coaching her to swap commands for how-about-we invitations.

passage:
On the terrace of their Mumbai building, Naveen's kite kept nose-diving into the water tanks. Irawati watched for ten seconds, then marched over. "You've tied the thread too high. And you're pulling too hard. And you should run the other way. Give it here."

Naveen yanked the reel back. "I didn't ask you!" He turned his back.

Irawati stood there, cheeks hot. She'd only wanted to help. She sat on the ledge and watched the kite crash twice more. This time she didn't march over. "Naveen? Would you like an idea, or do you want to figure it out yourself?"

Naveen sighed. "An idea. One."
"Tie the thread a bit lower."
He did. The kite climbed.

qa.q: Where did Naveen's kite keep nose-diving?
qa.a: Into the water tanks.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling after Naveen said, "I didn't ask you!"?
qa.a: Hurt and embarrassed, with hot cheeks, since she had only wanted to help.

qa.q: What made Irawati's second offer work?
qa.a: She asked first whether he wanted an idea and then gave just one, instead of a list of corrections 🙂

qa.q: How did Naveen experience Irawati's first burst of advice?
qa.a: It felt bossy, as if she was taking over his kite, so he yanked the reel back and turned away.

grounding: It shows a child's unasked-for advice feeling bossy to a friend, and asking would you like an idea working better.

passage: "Ganga, you asked me to knock before coming in while you change. Good. You're right to ask. Let me, your grandmother Dolma, tell you why I agree so fast. When I was eleven, in Gangtok, I kept a diary under my mattress. One day I found my mother reading it by the window. I didn't speak to her for two days. When your mother was your age, I promised I would never read her diary. But I also told her, 'Privacy is yours, but I must always know where you are and who you're with. That part is for safety.' So: I will knock, and I won't touch your notebook. And you will tell me when you go to your friend's house. Fair?"

qa.q: Where did young Dolma keep her diary?
qa.a: Under her mattress.

qa.q: How did young Dolma feel when she found her mother reading the diary?
qa.a: Betrayed and hurt, so upset that she didn't speak to her mother for two days.

qa.q: What choice did Dolma make later as a mother?
qa.a: She promised never to read her daughter's diary, but explained the safety limit: she must always know where she is and who she's with.

qa.q: How might Ganga's mother, as a girl, have felt about Dolma's promise?
qa.a: She likely felt trusted and respected, knowing her diary was her own, while understanding why her mother needed to know where she was.

grounding: It is a grandmother's memory explaining why she honours a child's request for privacy while keeping the safety limit of knowing where she is.

passage:
The monsoon storm had knocked the power out at the school hostel, and the girls wanted to watch the lightning from the roof. Warden Aunty stood at the stairs. "No roof tonight."

Shreya stamped. "That's so unfair!"

Kashish touched her arm, then turned to the warden. "Aunty, may I say something? We saw the Class 8 boys on their roof ten minutes ago. If they can go, why can't we?"

Warden Aunty raised her eyebrows. "Thank you for telling me politely. Nobody should be on any roof in lightning. It can strike the highest point." She called the boys' warden right then. "The answer stays no, for everyone. But you were right to object."

Kashish nodded. Shreya grumbled, but more quietly.

qa.q: Who had Kashish seen on their roof?
qa.a: The Class 8 boys, ten minutes earlier.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when she stamped and said, "That's so unfair!"?
qa.a: Frustrated and angry at being stopped, especially as it seemed a rule only for the girls.

qa.q: What made Kashish's objection effective?
qa.a: She asked politely, gave a specific fact about the boys and stayed calm, so the warden listened and fixed the unfairness.

qa.q: How did Warden Aunty see Kashish's objection?
qa.a: As fair and respectful; she thanked her, explained the lightning danger and called the boys' warden, even though the answer stayed no.

grounding: It shows a child objecting to unfair treatment with respectful words, and an adult supporting the objection while explaining why the roof stays forbidden.

passage:
All morning at the school sports day, Ganga kept checking the gate. Papa had said, "I promise. I'll be there for your relay, front row."

The relay started. The front row had Pooja's mother and Mariam's grandfather, but no Papa. Ganga ran her leg fast, handed on the baton, then sat under the tree and wouldn't eat her lunch.

At four, Jomon came through the gate, still in his hospital porter's uniform. He sat down beside her. "I broke my promise, and I'm sorry. They called me in for an emergency shift, and I couldn't get away. I should have phoned the school office to tell you."

Ganga didn't look at him. "You PROMISED."
"I know. Next time I'll only promise what I'm sure of."

qa.q: What was Jomon still wearing when he arrived?
qa.a: His hospital porter's uniform.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling as she sat under the tree and wouldn't eat?
qa.a: Deeply hurt and let down that Papa broke his promise to be in the front row.

qa.q: What did Jomon do that could help rebuild Ganga's trust?
qa.a: He apologised, explained honestly why he couldn't come, admitted he should have phoned, and promised to promise only what he is sure of.

qa.q: What was it like for Jomon to face Ganga's "You PROMISED"?
qa.a: Jomon knows he let her down, and he accepts her anger instead of arguing, which shows he takes the broken promise seriously.

grounding: It shows a child treating a parent's broken promise as a serious hurt, and the parent explaining honestly to rebuild trust.

passage:
After the temple fair, where a boy from the next village had played the harmonium so fast the crowd clapped along, Tanvir burst into the courtyard. "I'm going to practise every single day and be the best harmonium player in the whole district!"

His cousin Mahima, shelling peas, looked up. "Last month you were going to be the best kabaddi raider."

Tanvir scowled. "This is different."
"Okay. Then make it small. What will you practise tomorrow, and when?"
Tanvir thought. "The first line of the aarti tune. After milking, before school. Ten minutes."
"Write it on the wall calendar."

He did, in big crooked letters. Five mornings later, the first line of the aarti was floating across the courtyard, a little wobbly.

qa.q: Where did Tanvir write his plan?
qa.a: On the wall calendar, in big crooked letters.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when he burst into the courtyard?
qa.a: Excited and inspired after watching the harmonium player at the fair, eager to be the best 😊

qa.q: What turned Tanvir's big declaration into something that worked?
qa.a: Mahima helped him make it small and specific: the first line of the aarti tune, ten minutes after milking, written on the calendar.

qa.q: How did Mahima see Tanvir's big declaration?
qa.a: Mahima was doubtful, remembering last month's kabaddi plan, but still helped make it workable.

grounding: It shows a child declaring a big goal and a cousin helping turn it into a small, specific plan that succeeds.

passage:
Monday: Tarun, new from Bihar, ate his lunch alone on the steps again. Sachin picked up his tiffin and sat beside him. "Is that litti? My Nani makes it." Tarun's face opened like a window.

Wednesday: Near the cycle stand, two Class 8 boys grabbed Tarun's cap and held it high. "Say please in Bhojpuri!" Sachin stepped in. "Give it back." One shoved him hard. Sachin didn't shove back. He ran straight to the PT teacher, Mr Sequeira, who came at once, got the cap back and took both boys to the office.

Friday: In assembly, Mr Sequeira said, "Standing by a friend is brave. Getting an adult when it turns rough is braver still." Sachin and Tarun, sharing a bench, tried not to grin.

qa.q: What was Tarun eating on Monday?
qa.a: Litti.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when Sachin sat beside him on Monday?
qa.a: Relieved and happy to have company after eating alone, and less lonely as a newcomer.

qa.q: Why was running to Mr Sequeira the right move on Wednesday?
qa.a: Once the older boys shoved him, it was unsafe to handle alone; fetching the PT teacher protected both boys and got the cap back.

qa.q: How did Mr Sequeira view Sachin's actions?
qa.a: He saw both standing by a friend and fetching an adult as brave, and praised fetching an adult as braver still.

grounding: It shows a child sitting with a lonely classmate and standing up for him, then getting an adult when it turns unsafe, and being praised for both.

passage:
On the second night at the lakeside camp in Scotland, Yara lay in her bunk with her face pressed into Mum's old blue scarf, the one that still smelled of their kitchen. Her throat ached. She could picture Dad burning the pancakes on Saturday, her little brother's socks everywhere.

Freya, the camp leader, found her by torchlight. "Missing home?" Yara nodded into the scarf. Freya sat on the floor by the bunk. "That ache means you've got people worth missing. Tell me one thing you'd be doing right now."
"Fighting with my brother over the TV."
They both laughed a little. "Your call home is booked for six tomorrow. Keep the scarf close till then."

Yara breathed in the kitchen smell and, eventually, slept.

qa.q: What did Yara press her face into?
qa.a: Mum's old blue scarf.

qa.q: What was Yara feeling on the second night?
qa.a: Homesick and longing for her family, with an aching throat as she pictured home.

qa.q: What three things did Freya use to help?
qa.a: She got Yara talking about home, encouraged her to keep the comfort scarf close, and reminded her of the call booked for six tomorrow.

qa.q: How did Freya see Yara's homesickness?
qa.a: As a healthy sign that Yara has people worth missing, not something to be ashamed of.

grounding: It shows a child homesick at camp, eased by talking, a comfort item and a planned call, with missing family framed as healthy attachment.
